https://telex.hu/karakter/konyvespolc/20.text: Menü Kereső Erdős Virág: Az ember lelke legmélyét is megmérgezte a rendszer, amiben 16 évig éltünk Könyvespolc Videó Interjú Podcast Nyáry Krisztián „Azt éreztem, hogy mindig tilalomfalakba ütközött az ember” – mondta Erdős Virág a Buksó legújabb epizódjában a kortárs magyar irodalom állapotáról, amely szerinte nem teljesítette azt a küldetését, hogy a társadalmi változásoknak valós előmozdítója legyen. „Én azon az állásponton voltam, hogy szerintem azért ebben több lehetőség lett volna. Közben azért látjuk, hogy tizenhat évig mélyült ez a hatalmas gödör” – tette hozzá a József Attila-díjas költő, aki egyebek mellett saját közéleti aktivista múltját is kritizálta, és arról is megnyílt, miért terhes számára szerzőként minden nyilvános szereplés. Bár Erdős Virág nem kedveli a rivaldafényt, ezért nagyon ritkán is ad interjút, Nyáry Krisztiánnal kivételt tett. „Nekem alapból bajom van ezzel a fajta nyilvánossággal, amibe bele vagyunk vetve, én másfajta működésre vagyok szocializálva. Hirtelen lettünk beletéve ezekbe a nyilvános terekbe, ahol az ember azt érzi, hogy elvész a lényeg. Megjelenik az embernek egy könyve, és rögtön utána futni kell három-négy helyre, hogy meséljek arról, amit most írtam meg. Minthogyha a könyv helyett beszélnénk.” A népszerűség, az ismertség önmagában kevés, jóllehet az irodalomnak szüksége van olvasókra ahhoz, hogy be tudjon tölteni társadalmi vagy esztétikai szerepeket. „Szerintem kezdettől fogva nagyobb csapda volt a bulvár felé engedni magunkat, mint adott esetben társadalmi változásokat szorgalmazni. Ez egy annyira fura dinamika, mert minél inkább törekszünk arra, hogy sokan olvassanak minket, annál inkább válunk mosóporrá, ami minden alkalommal ugyanolyan jól fog mosni” – mondta a költő. A beszélgetés fontosabb gondolatait ebben a cikkben szövegesen is összefoglaltuk. A következő adás két hét múlva, szeptember 8-án érkezik, addig is iratkozzon fel a Buksó új Spotify-csatornájára. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

https://www.stratford-herald.com/news/ki.text: Home News Article The story of designer Tibor Reich, along with samples of some of his fabrics, is included in the Stratford Heritage Exhibition in Harvard House on Stratford High Street By Stratford News Editor - news@stratford-herald.com Published: 05:01, 31 August 2026 As I gaze upon any of the designs – textiles or ceramics – by Tibor Reich (1916-1996) it feels as though I am looking forwards and backwards, writes Paul Edmondson. I can easily appreciate how modern he must have seemed in his own time. My response to Reich’s work is surely revealing of his qualities as a designer. Tibor Reich, 1957. He was born in Budapest to a wealthy family of industrial weavers. At the age of 21, he fled Nazi persecution and came to England to study textiles at Leeds University. Six years later, he married professional pianist Freda Caplan, and they settled in Clifford Chambers in the year after the war. There his industry flourished and grew to employ a staff of 80. He was an innovator and carried the famous Bauhaus influence with him throughout his career: modernist, originally artistic, functional, and mass-produced. He invented ‘deep textured weaves’ which brought to textiles an impression of three dimensions. His ‘fotextur’ technique took inspiration from negative and positive photographic prints of the natural world and objects. Reich commemorated and celebrated. He designed ‘Princess’ for the royal wedding in 1947, and among his major commissions were designs for Coventry Cathedral, the upholstery for Concorde, and textiles for the QE2. For the royal opening of The Shakespeare Centre: Reich’s ‘Age of Kings’ (1964). Photo: SBT But Stratford, which became his home, is blessed indeed with its share of his designs. Among his textiles in 1964 were the ‘Age of Kings’, ‘Midsummer Night’s Dream’, ‘Hathaway’, ‘The Battle of Agincourt’, and ‘Verona’ for the new Shakespeare Centre. In 1969, he produced tea towels based on ‘Richard II’ and ‘The Taming of The Shrew’, a fabric picture of Shakespeare and David Garrick, and his wall-hanging, ‘The Garrick Jubilee’, to mark the 200th anniversary of that great Stratford-upon-Avon occasion. Reich was fascinated by colour as well as by texture, which means his designs remain vibrant and alive, calling us back to the past, and shining – ever-modern – in our present. The story of Reich, along with samples of some of his fabrics, is included in the Stratford Heritage Exhibition in Harvard House on High Street, Thursday to Sunday, 10.30am-3.30pm, until 27th September. All are welcome. Admission is free. The exhibition is presented by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and Stratford Society and based on the research of Jann Tracy. Image caption: For the Royal opening of The Shakespeare Centre: Reich’s ‘Age of Kings’ (1964). Copyright: Tibor Reich Designs Ltd. Image: The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: A top Kremlin chief has issued a chilling warning that a major European nation could be wiped off the map "in a few days" if it picks a fight with Russia. Presidential aide Nikolai Patrushev said that Poland would face total annihilation in an apparent nuclear warning, according to Russian outlet Izvestia. Patrushev said: "If Poland enters into military operations against Russia, our country will use the entire arsenal of its available forces and means, and Polish statehood will cease to exist in 2-3 days." The terrifying threat comes hot on the heels of a Russian drone strike hitting a railway line in western Ukraine, blowing up a train just miles from the Polish border. Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson was travelling towards Poland after attending a security conference in Kyiv when the incident occurred, reports the Express . He is understood to have escaped unharmed. Former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt was among those on the train with Mr Johnson. "This wasn't our train [that was hit], but the one just minutes after us by the [Polish] border crossing," he said. It was evacuated as the [Russian] drone approached, and no one was hurt." Tensions are high as Russia has recently intensified its attacks on border crossing areas in western Ukraine in a bid to disrupt Kyiv's logistics. In one of these attacks, the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing, a key link between Ukraine and Poland, was also hit. There are fears that Russia could escalate the conflict, especially with several reports of Russian drones entering NATO countries' airspace. The most recent incidents involved NATO fighter jets have been scrambled above Lithuania tonight to intercept a drone. The country's president, Gitanas Nauseda, appeared to indirectly blame Russia. Writing on X, he said: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets. I thank Allied personnel for their swift response. With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace." Last week, a Russian drone was reportedly spotted flying over Moldova and towards Romania as Bucharest issued an urgent security alert. A drone allegedly also entered Moldova's airspace, and the country's Defence Ministry said in a statement that it was a "Shahed-type" which entered the airspace from the "direction of Ukraine".
